5237.prule: No stress rule stated. Sibine (Somrai) is described with three contrastive level tones, high, mid and low, plus complex low-high and high-low tones; lexical tone is one of the five criteria that define verb classes, with minimal sets such as ʔyá 'tuer' (H) / ʔyā 'se coucher' (M) / yà 'donner naissance' (B) and ʔásá 'tousser' / ʔāsā 'compter' / ʔàsà 'jeter', and tone alternations mark aspect (aorist, accompli, verbal noun, subjunctive). Stress, accent and intensity are never mentioned in the chapter's phonological preliminary (syllable structure CV/CVC, consonants, three central vowels, tones) or anywhere else in it.

5238.heavy: "Exceptions to this regular pattern are caused in the first place by the existence of bimoraic syllables, which appear to be the strongest stress attractor." (p. 83)... "(C)VN syllables, which are considered heavier than (C)V syllables by J. Payne (1991:11) and Crowhurst & Michael (2005:56-57), do not change the regular stress pattern" (p. 84)... "in terms of vocalic quality, /a/-syllables are the heaviest and /i/-syllables the weakest" (p. 91, point 7).
5238.dflt: disyllables: 1st syllable; 3-4 syllables: 2nd syllable; 5-6 syllables: primary on 2nd, secondary on 4th; 7+ syllables: no regular iambic pattern (pp. 83, 86, 88-90)
5238.prule: Stress is non-phonemic and follows tendencies rather than rigid rules. Default (no bimoraic syllable): the final syllable is extrametrical and iambic disyllabic feet are built from the left, so disyllables are stressed on the 1st syllable and words of 3-6 syllables on the 2nd (= penult in 2-3-syllable words, antepenult in 4-syllable words). A bimoraic syllable (long vowel or diphthong) anywhere in the word is the strongest stress attractor and takes the primary (or at least a secondary) stress, even in disyllables and even word-finally (rowáe 'he eats us', róotaki 'that is', otháwinatakàe 'it has cursed us'). (C)VN syllables do NOT count as heavy (antaki, antami, antawo keep 2nd-syllable stress). Vowel quality acts as a weaker gradient: /a/-syllables attract stress (especially word-initially: hápokana, páminìro) and /i/-syllables repel it. In words of seven or more syllables the iambic pattern no longer operates regularly (author's summary, 2.5.4).
5238.srule: Penta- and hexasyllabic words with no bimoraic syllable: primary on the 2nd syllable, secondary on the 4th (okématzìri, ikántanàkiro). A bimoraic first syllable takes the primary and a secondary tends to fall on the 3rd (káakitàki, náakatàki); when a later bimoraic syllable takes the primary, the first foot gets a secondary (ròmaryáaka, nèwatyéero) - disyllabic feet tend not to stay unstressed. Word-final enclitics (demonstrative enclitics, conditional =rika, locative =ki, plural =paeni, exclamative =wee) and the possessive suffixes -ni/-ti tend to carry a secondary stress (fn. 35 p. 85; 2.5.4 point 6). The counter-expectative enclitic =maita carries its own primary stress (téemáita, káarimáita = two phonological words). The author states that the primary/secondary distinction is auditory and tentative (fn. 33, p. 81).

qtr.text: 5 Tonology 5.1 The tones. The tonology of Nizaa is relatively complex. ... Nizaa has a tone system with three distinctive pitch levels: H(igh), M(id) and B (= Low). The opposition between M and Low is subordinate to that between H and non-H ... But Nizaa does not have only the three tones H, M and Low. Leaving aside downstep and floating tones, nine different tones must be distinguished for an adequate description. Besides the three simple tones H, M and Low, there are five double tones, HM, HB, MH, MB and BH, and one triple tone, BHM.

5239.dq: No sentence in the article mentions accent, stress or prominence (accent / intensité / proéminence / tonique absent from all 13 pages); word prosody is described only as lexical tone: 'Le nizaa a un système tonologique à trois hauteurs distinctives: H(aut), M(oyen) et B(as).'
5239.prule: none stated: lexical tone language (3 levels, 9 lexical noun tones); the source gives no stress or accent rule
5239.quote: 5 La tonologie 5.1 Les tons La tonologie du nizaa est relativement complexe. ... Le nizaa a un système tonologique à trois hauteurs distinctives: H(aut), M(oyen) et B(as). L'opposition entre M et B est subordonnée à celle entre H et non-H ... Mais le nizaa n'a pas seulement les trois tons H, M et B. En negligeant le downstep et les tons flottants, il nous faut distinguer neuf tons différents pour obtenir une description suffisante. Outre les trois tons simples, H, M et B, il s'agit de cinq tons doubles, HM, HB, MH, MB et BH, et un ton triple, BHM.
5239.loc: sect. 5 'La tonologie', 5.1 'Les tons', p. 43; supporting: 5.2 'Le downstep' p. 46, 5.3 'La tonologie des substantifs polysyllabiques' p. 47, sect. 1.2 rule (1.3) 'Un substantif doit contenir au moins deux mores' p. 32
5239.tone: Theil 1992 (first and only full phonology of Nizaa; fieldwork Galim 1983-84) describes word prosody exclusively as tone: three distinctive levels H, M, B (M vs B subordinate to H vs non-H); nine lexical tones on monosyllabic nouns (H, M, B, HM, HB, MH, MB, BH, BHM) plus floating H (Ho, Mo, Bo classes, 10 lexical classes in table 5.3); downstep !H (rule 5.9); 'transport des tons' = shift of a syllable's final tone onto the following syllable (5.6); definite form of nouns = suffixed B tone (5.7); polysyllabic nouns carry any of the ten lexical tones on the FINAL syllable and only H, M, B, BH on non-final syllables (5.3, p. 47). Monosyllabic verbs contrast only H vs non-H. Nowhere does the article mention accent, stress or syllable prominence: no stress rule and no denial of stress. Kjelsvik 2002 (MA, sect. 2.1.5 'Tones') and Kjelsvik 2008 (PhD, 4.4.2 'Tones': 'a rich tonology, with three distinctive tonelevels and a number of tone combinations used as lexical tones... tones are regularily transported') likewise describe only tone and defer to this article; PHOIBLE 1317 lists H, M, L and contours.

It is worth noting that modern Sui itself is not entirely monosyllabic. Our wordlist includes several glosses which elicited iambic sesquisyllabic forms in various locations. [pp.23-24]
5240.prule: No word-stress rule stated: Sui is a tone language (6 tones on unchecked + 2 on checked syllables) and 'essentially monosyllabic'. 5242.dq: Tone patterns extending over phonological words mark case in nouns and tense in verbs. (M. C. Schröder 2004: 30) / ...it falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in non-past tense. (Schröder & Schröder 1984: 46 n. 3) -- the tonal statements are made over the word; no word- or phrase-level stress/prominence domain is described anywhere.
5242.prule: No word-stress rule is stated in any opened Toposa description (Schröder & Schröder 1984; H. Schröder 2002, 2004, 2013; M. C. Schröder 2004, 2026): the words 'stress' and 'accent' (as prominence) do not occur. Toposa is described as a tone language: high and low tones, a fall at the end of words and a rare word-final rise, a mid tone as a variant of H, raised H / lowered L from morphotonemics (Schröder 2002: 19); 'Tone in Toposa is grammatical rather than lexical. Tone patterns extending over phonological words mark case in nouns and tense in verbs' (M. C. Schröder 2004: 30). The only positional statement is tonal and hedged: on most verbs the high tone falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in non-past tense and on the final syllable in past tense, 'very tentative' (Schröder & Schröder 1984: 9, 46 n. 3).
5242.quote: [p. 9] In the past tense, high tone occurs on the final syllable rather than on the penultimate syllable as in non-past.³ ... [p. 46 n. 3] In most verbs the high tone seems predictable in so far as it falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in non-past tense. In past tense it falls on the final syllable. This description is very tentative yet and awaits further tonal analysis. For this reason high tone is only indicated when the contrast between past and non-past, is in focus. ... [M. 5242.exq_: In most verbs the high tone seems predictable ... This description is very tentative yet and awaits further tonal analysis. (1984: 46 n. 3; a hedge on the tonal placement, not on a stress rule)
5242.tone: Two-level tone system (H, L; word-final F and rare R; M as a variant of H) with grammatical function: tone patterns over the phonological word mark case on nouns (e.g. nominative pattern on nyaberu 'woman') and tense on verbs. Verb H tone is described as largely predictable by tense: penultimate syllable in non-past, final syllable in past (1984: 9, 46 n. 3, explicitly tentative; H 'marked with the acute accent' only where the past/non-past contrast is in focus). No source describes stress, accent or any non-tonal word prominence; M. C. Schröder 2004: 30 reports a rejected orthography proposal to mark tense with an acute on the verb's last syllable 'irrespective of the tone on that particular syllable'.

Due to morphotonemics, raised highs and lowered lows also occur ... qtr.text: On the stressing of words: in Pidgin the accent mostly rests on the first syllable, however long the word is (singsing, gáramut, sánguma = dance feast, slit drum, black magic). In the vernacular languages [Ak and Auwon] the stress in disyllabic words lies without exception on the first syllable, whereas in two-[sic; evidently three-] and polysyllabic words it shifts to the second syllable. 5255.dq: Statements concern lexical tone on nouns/verbs (word level) and grammatical tone over the 'verb word' (subject index + root + suffixes) within clauses; data are elicited sentence paradigms with tone letters plus narrative clips, transcribed in the 2018 Dadiya orthography (which marks H only on two subject indexes jə́, ń).
5255.prule: Dadiya is tonal: two tone levels (H, L) with automatic and non-automatic downstep of H; lexical tone is contrastive on nouns (minimal pairs) and at least some verbs (dʊ́wá 'carry!' vs dʊ̀wà 'flex!'), while tone melodies on the verb word mark aspect (progressive/perfective: tone spreads from the subject index; future: H on verb; habitual: L on verb). Nothing is said about word stress or accent anywhere in the paper (full-text search: 'stress' 0, 'accent' only in 'acute accent diacritic').
5255.srule: not discussed (no stress discussed at all)

5259.prule: Impressionistic tendency statement: in (lowland) Gaddang the accent 'frequently' falls on the first syllable of the word -- all 15 illustrative words are disyllables, so = penult (áfuy, tólay, ának, úlu, máta...), contrasted with Yogad/Ibanag where accent is 'frequently' on the second (final) syllable of the same etyma. evidence_works.detail: Counts 50 elicited words (27 'common', 23 'not common') by the syllable said to bear stress, counted from the left: 1st 27 (54 %), 2nd 15 (30 %), 3rd 4 (8 %), 'undifferentiated' 4 (8 %; interjections and phrases such as Dios Mabbalat) (Table 5, p. 26); 'majority of these gaddang terms are being stressed in the first syllable like "afak/afac", in which the first letter 'a' is given emphasis' (p. 26); 'Majority of the identified gaddang terms are functioning as noun and being stressed on their first syllable' (p. 27). Sample marked forms: Afak/Afac, Di'os Mab'balat, Fu'tuk, Kap'pakel, Payàw (Table 3, p. 25); Attung at Alo, Bal'ya'wan, Karangàt, Maca'pang'ua, Pàtta (Table 4, p. 26). Because the tally is from the word's beginning over items of two to five syllables, it does not convert into penult/final figures; it shows stress distributed over positions with no rule and a word-initial majority in this elicited set, which matches Galang 1935's 'accent frequently appears on the first syllable' (record.quote) and is compatible with the lexical coding proposed under the KWF row. evidence_works.detail: Table 1 (p. 5): '(H) Paroxytone = accent (with or without secondary vowel lengthening) falling regularly on the penult: Gaddang, Makassarese, Paiwan, Pazeh-Kahabu, Ishbukun-Bunun, Maanyan'; Yogad under '(G) Oxytone = accent... falling regularly on the ultima'. Zorc qualifies the table on the same page: 'Such a classification may be more useful on given words, rather than on languages as a whole, although in some cases only one or two statements may apply... I would like to be able to make a comprehensive list of AN languages on this basis, and insure the accuracy of statements in Table 1. I would deeply appreciate your assistance in achieving this goal.' p. 6: 'Drift can also account for the appearance of long vowels. Gaddang dialects (McFarland 1977) generally have long penult vowels when followed by a single consonant, even though surrounding languages have historically-derivable short vowels: Gad ma:ta 'eye' < PPH *matá, Gad bi:fig 'lip' < PPH *bibíR, Gad diwa:nan < PNC *di-wanán 'right (hand)', GadS ku:ku 'fingernail' < PPH *kukúh, Gad li:kud 'back' < PPH *likúd, Gad da:pan 'sole' < PNP *dapán, etc.' In Zorc's framework penult length is the correlate of word accent, so this says lowland Gaddang has regularised penult length (his 'secondary vowel lengthening') even on etyma with PPH final accent; the data are McFarland's length-transcribed wordlists, which carry no stress statement.

(3) The development of contrastive accent could have been a dialectal feature of PPH, and languages like Ivatan, Tausug, Pangasinan, and Gaddang are all survivors of dialects in which such contrasts were not made, while Ilokano, Ibanag, Ifugao, Tagalog, and Hanunoo are all survivors of dialects where contrasts were made.' 5262.prule: The author transcribes his first-hand Gvoko lexical data with a two-way tone marking (high á vs low à), i.e. treats Gvoko (like Dghwede and Guduf) as a tone language with at least H and L; tone is left unmarked in the sentence examples for lack of reliable data, especially for Gvoko. No analysis of the tonal system (number of contrastive tones, downstep, functional load) and nothing at all about word stress or accent.

tn.translation: fn.11: Newman's Proto-Chadic *hl (voiceless lateral fricative) is unified as IPA *ɬ here for readability, e.g. item 1 'to answer' *hləwə > *ɬəwə. High tone is marked (á), low tone (à). ... fn.15: Owing to the limitations of the data (especially Gvoko), tone marking is omitted in these morpho-syntactic example sentences.
